back:
Fully managed, serverless key-value/document NoSQL database with single-digit-millisecond latency at any scale, with no server or cluster to provision or patch.

Data is organized into tables of items (rows) with attributes (columns), addressed by a primary key that's either a simple partition key or a composite partition key plus sort key — there's no fixed schema beyond the key attributes, so items in the same table can otherwise carry different attributes.

front: DynamoDB: Partition Keys and Hot Partitions
back:
DynamoDB spreads a table's data and throughput across partitions based on a hash of the partition key — choosing a key with high cardinality and even access distribution is what lets a table actually achieve its provisioned or on-demand throughput.

Hot partition: when one partition key value (or a small number of them) receives disproportionately more reads/writes than others — e.g. a low-cardinality key like a status flag, or a naturally popular value like one trending product ID — that single partition throttles long before the table's overall capacity is exhausted.

Mitigation: pick a high-cardinality partition key (e.g. a user ID, or a composite key), or apply write sharding — appending a random or calculated suffix to a hot key value to spread its items across multiple physical partitions — when the natural key can't avoid concentration.

front: DynamoDB: Global Secondary Index (GSI) vs. Local Secondary Index (LSI)
back:
Global Secondary Index (GSI): a different partition key (and optional sort key) than the base table, with its own provisioned throughput — lets you query the same data by an entirely different access pattern. Can be added or removed after table creation, and reads from it are always eventually consistent.

Local Secondary Index (LSI): the same partition key as the base table, but a different sort key — supports strongly consistent reads, but must be created at table creation time (never added later) and shares the base table's throughput.

Exam trigger: 'need a new query pattern on an existing, already-populated table' points to a GSI, since an LSI can never be added retroactively.

front: DynamoDB: Capacity Modes — On-Demand vs. Provisioned
back:
Provisioned capacity: you specify Read/Write Capacity Units (RCUs/WCUs) ahead of time, optionally paired with Application Auto Scaling to adjust them within a defined range based on utilization — cheaper at steady, predictable load, but under-provisioning causes throttling and over-provisioning wastes cost.

On-demand capacity: no capacity planning at all — DynamoDB scales instantly to accommodate traffic and bills per request, at a higher per-request cost — the answer whenever a scenario describes unpredictable or spiky traffic and wants to eliminate throttling risk without manual tuning.

Exam trigger: 'traffic is unpredictable and we keep getting throttled' or 'we don't want to manage capacity at all' points to on-demand; a well-known, steady baseline load favors provisioned with auto scaling for cost efficiency.

An ordered, time-sequenced log of item-level changes (inserts, updates, deletes) in a table, retained for 24 hours — lets other services react to data changes without polling the table directly.

Commonly consumed by a Lambda function (triggered automatically per shard) to replicate changes elsewhere, maintain a derived or aggregated view, or fan out an event for other systems to react to — the same underlying mechanism that powers DynamoDB Global Tables' cross-Region replication.

Active-active, multi-Region replication for a DynamoDB table — every replica Region can accept both reads and writes, with changes propagating to other Regions typically within a second, built on top of DynamoDB Streams.

Exam trigger: a global application needing low-latency reads and writes from multiple Regions simultaneously, or cross-Region disaster recovery with near-zero RPO — this is DynamoDB's answer for multi-Region needs, since it has no separate cross-region read-replica feature the way RDS/Aurora do.

Conflict resolution uses 'last writer wins' based on timestamps, so applications with concurrent cross-Region writes to the same item need to tolerate that resolution model.

A fully managed, write-through in-memory cache sitting directly in front of DynamoDB, dropping read latency from single-digit milliseconds down to microseconds for repeated reads of the same items, while also reducing read capacity consumed on the underlying table.

Accessed via a DAX client that's largely API-compatible with the standard DynamoDB SDK, so adopting it typically requires minimal application code changes — the standard answer whenever a scenario has a small hot set of frequently-read items and needs microsecond-level latency without re-architecting.

TransactWriteItems and TransactGetItems group up to 100 actions across one or more tables into a single all-or-nothing operation, with full ACID guarantees — every action succeeds together, or none of them apply.

Exam trigger: 'update multiple items atomically' or 'enforce a rule across more than one item/table' (e.g. moving funds between two account items, or enforcing a uniqueness constraint) — a plain BatchWriteItem has no such atomicity, since it just batches independent writes that can partially succeed.

Transactions consume roughly double the throughput of the equivalent non-transactional operation, since DynamoDB performs two underlying steps (prepare and commit) per item.

Automatically deletes items past a Unix timestamp stored in a designated attribute, at no additional cost and without consuming write capacity for the deletion — typically within 48 hours of expiration, not instantly.

Exam trigger: 'automatically expire old data' — session data, temporary tokens, or time-bound records — without a scheduled job or Lambda function to scan for and delete expired items yourself. TTL deletions also flow through DynamoDB Streams, so an expiring item can still trigger downstream processing (e.g. archiving to S3) before it's gone.

front: DynamoDB Backups: On-Demand vs. Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR)
back:
On-demand backups: a full backup of a table at a specific point in time, retained until explicitly deleted, with no performance impact on the table — the choice for long-term archival or a specific pre-change snapshot.

Point-in-time recovery (PITR): continuous backups letting you restore a table to any second within the last 35 days once enabled, similar in spirit to RDS automated backups — the answer whenever a scenario needs to recover from an accidental write or delete to some specific recent moment, not just a scheduled snapshot.

Both restore to a new table, never in place — restoring never overwrites the existing table.

front: DynamoDB: Eventually Consistent vs. Strongly Consistent Reads
back:
By default, DynamoDB reads are eventually consistent — a read shortly after a write might return stale data, since it could be served from a replica that hasn't caught up yet. Requesting a strongly consistent read (available on the base table and LSIs, never on a GSI) guarantees the most up-to-date data, at roughly double the read capacity cost and slightly higher latency.

Exam trigger: 'must always read the absolute latest value immediately after a write' points to strongly consistent reads — but remember a GSI can never provide one, since it's a separate, asynchronously updated index.

front: DynamoDB: Item Size Limit and Design Implications
back:
A single item — all its attributes combined — is capped at 400 KB, with no way to raise this limit, so it directly shapes data modeling: large binary blobs, big documents, or unbounded lists/sets don't belong directly in an item.

Common workaround: store the large object in S3 and keep only a reference (the S3 key or URL) in the DynamoDB item — the pattern whenever a scenario describes large attachments or large payloads alongside DynamoDB metadata.

Instead of one table per entity type (customers, orders, order items), a single table stores multiple related entity types together, using composite (often generic, like PK/SK) partition and sort keys structured around the application's known access patterns.

The payoff: related items — e.g. a customer and all their orders — can be retrieved in one Query call instead of multiple round trips across separate tables, since DynamoDB has no native joins; minimizing round trips this way is central to designing performant, cost-efficient access patterns.

Trade-off: it only pays off when access patterns are known upfront and stable — ad hoc or frequently changing query needs are usually better served by a more normalized, multi-table design, or a different database entirely.

front: DynamoDB vs. RDS/Aurora — how do you choose?
back: Choose based on access pattern: DynamoDB for key-value lookups at massive scale with careful partition-key design (to avoid hot partitions); RDS/Aurora when you need complex joins or multi-table transactions.
